eh_study.title: Run an Energy Hub reference-design study
eh_study.intro: An Energy Hub study sizes a site behind its grid connection to an availability target, then tells you — section by section — what it could and could not establish. This tour walks through each control once.

steps.title: 1 · Choose the archetype pack
steps.body: The pack is the planning situation: strong_grid (imports freely), weak_flexible (capped import, SCR gate, DSR opt-in) or off_grid (the import Links are islanded). It sets the ENS target, the LOLE certification rule and the default stages.
steps.enter: Pick the situation that matches the site's grid connection. A template project preselects it for you.

steps.title: 2 · Template recommendation
steps.body: Projects made from an Energy Hub template carry a recommended pack, settings and study notes. 'Use recommended settings' fills the form in one click.
steps.enter: Optional — only shown for template projects.

steps.title: 3 · Check readiness before you run
steps.body: Readiness is a free preview: which Links count as imports and by which rule, the critical buses, the hub boundary the MC uses, and a per-stage prediction of what will run, be skipped (and why) and how many LP solves it costs.
steps.enter: Fix any 'not established' reason here (usually a missing tag) before spending solves.

steps.title: 4 · Pack settings
steps.body: Blank fields keep the pack's own values. Everything you set here is validated before the study starts — nothing is silently ignored.
steps.enter: Open it to adjust targets, the budget, MC draws, DSR buses, the energy import budget, levers and stages.

steps.title: 5 · Targets and budget
steps.body: ENS target (‱ of energy demand unserved) drives the capacity expansion; LOLE target (h/yr) is what the Monte-Carlo certifies against; Budget caps the LP solves across all stages; Import cap / Import energy (weak_flexible) limit grid imports in MW and MWh/yr.
steps.enter: Typical: ENS 1–10 ‱, LOLE 3 h/yr, budget 30–60 solves.

steps.title: 6 · DtC attribution
steps.body: Design-to-critical (DtC) islands the import and checks critical demand. 'By bus' counts every Load on a critical bus; 'Per Load' reports each critical Load and sheds non-critical Loads first (a disclosed 5 % VOLL priority, exact on loss-free paths).
steps.enter: Use Per Load when critical and non-critical Loads share a bus.

steps.title: 7 · Levers
steps.body: The levers stage compares design options at the same target: storage duration, import cap, energy import budget, redundancy. 'pack' keeps the archetype's own choice.
steps.enter: Turn on the levers you want priced; each option costs one solve.

steps.title: 8 · Stages
steps.body: apply_pack → ens_solve → frontier → mc_certify → fmea_top → redundancy → levers → dtc_stress → dtc_planning → assemble. Untick 'pack's default stages' to choose; the required ones always run.
steps.enter: Readiness updates as you change stages, so you see the solve cost first.

steps.title: 9 · Run
steps.body: The study runs on a private copy — your network and solver settings are never changed. You can abort; solves already spent are kept and reported.
steps.enter: Press Run; progress appears here.

steps.title: 10 · Read the completeness chips
steps.body: Each section is ok (evidence produced), skipped (not requested or not applicable) or not established (requested but could not be shown — the reason is listed). A missing number is never reported as zero.
steps.enter: Start with the not-established reasons: they are your to-do list.

steps.title: 11 · Certification verdict
steps.body: Certified only when the MC LOLE 95 % confidence interval lies entirely below the target (pass). Fail = entirely above; inconclusive = the interval straddles it (more draws help).
steps.enter: Fail: tighten the energy target or add firm capacity, then ask the assistant for a reviewed recommendation. Inconclusive is not a failure: raise MC draws (Pack settings → Draws) or tighten the plan.

steps.title: 12 · Pipeline
steps.body: Every stage with its status (run / skipped / failed / aborted), the LP solves it charged and its note — the audit trail of the study.
steps.enter: Open it when a section is not established to see which stage said why.

steps.title: 13 · Export
steps.body: Download JSON saves the stored report exactly as the API serves it; Summary CSV flattens the headline, completeness and notes for a spreadsheet.
steps.enter: Exports are disabled after a later solve cleared the stored report — re-run the study.

fmea.title: Rank failure modes in the FMEA worksheet
fmea.intro: The worksheet ranks failure modes by expected cost per year (criticality = occurrence × severity). Classes A–C are computed by engines; class D rows are your expert judgement.

steps.title: 1 · Run the B/C sweep
steps.body: Class B re-solves each Link outage that carries outage data; class C re-solves each stress scenario below. Capacities are frozen at the plan, and the network is restored afterwards.
steps.enter: Needs VOLL > 0 in the solver settings; costs one solve per contingency.

steps.title: 2 · Read the ranking
steps.body: Class A = generator forced outages (analytic COPT screening); B = Link outages (LP re-solve); C = stress scenarios; D = expert rows. The badge names the engine and its fidelity — none of these is a statutory reliability figure.
steps.enter: Sort by criticality (€/yr) to see where risk concentrates.

steps.title: 3 · Mitigability
steps.body: The one editable cell on computed rows. What you type is stored with the project and survives re-solves (it is an overlay, not a row edit).
steps.enter: e.g. 'N+1 genset', 'spare transformer on site', 'accept'.

steps.title: 4 · Add an expert (class D) mode
steps.body: For risks no engine models — cyber, fuel supply, cooling plant. Criticality is computed from what you enter; the row is badged 'expert' and never impersonates an engine.
steps.enter: Name, events/yr, severity in €, optional mitigability.

steps.title: 5 · Stress scenarios (class C)
steps.body: Correlated weather/demand extremes that independent outage draws cannot compose. Parametric scenarios scale electrical load (0–10×) and profile-borne renewable availability (0–1.5×); profiles scenarios swap whole series from a pack.
steps.enter: Frequency is the empirical events per year, in (0, 365].

steps.title: 6 · Add a scenario
steps.body: Bounds are checked as you type; the server's message is shown verbatim if it still refuses. A profile pack must name Loads/Generators that exist on your network, or the sweep reports it incomplete.
steps.enter: e.g. heatwave: load ×1.15, renewables ×0.85, 0.3 /yr.

eh_tagging.title: Tag your network for an Energy Hub study
eh_tagging.intro: Four bus tags and one Link role tell the study where the grid ends, what must stay on, and how strong the connection is. Select a bus or a Link on the map to see these fields in the Properties panel.

steps.title: 1 · Bus tags
steps.body: Point of connection = the GRID-side bus of the import; Critical bus = its demand must be served when islanded; Short-circuit level and IBR capacity feed the SCR (grid-strength) gate at the PoC.
steps.enter: Select a bus, open Edit, then tick/enter the Energy Hub fields. Then select the import Link, open Edit and set its Energy Hub role — the tour adds that step as soon as a Link's Edit form is open.

steps.title: 2 · Link role
steps.body: Select the import Link on the map to see this field (the tour opens a bus first). grid_import marks the import Link the packs cap or island. Conversion roles (electrolyser, fuel_cell, conversion) identify units for redundancy scenarios and the multi-energy report.
steps.enter: Select the import Link, open Edit, choose grid_import.

hub_design.title: Design a hub in five steps
hub_design.intro: Five cards take you from an example site to a checked design. Each card asks for at most three choices, and the assistant can do any step for you.

steps.title: 1 · The five steps
steps.body: Start, Site, Goal, Results and Improve. Start, Site and Goal are open at any time; Results and Improve open once a study has finished. A tick marks a step that is done.

steps.title: 2 · Pick a starting point
steps.body: Each example site comes ready to study, with made-up but realistic data. You can also work on the network you already have.

steps.title: 3 · Check the site
steps.body: What the study needs to know: the grid connection, the load that must stay on, grid strength and how often equipment breaks. Anything missing has a fix button that asks the assistant.

steps.title: 4 · Say how the site meets the grid
steps.body: A strong grid you can always import from, a weak or limited connection, or no grid at all. This choice decides which checks the study runs.

steps.title: 5 · Set your goal
steps.body: How many hours per year some demand may go unserved. The example sites fill in a usual value; leave it empty to see the shortfall without a pass or fail answer.
steps.enter: 3 hours per year is a common planning goal.

steps.title: 6 · Run the study
steps.body: The study sizes the equipment, then tests the design against random breakdowns. It takes a few minutes; the rail moves on when it finishes.

steps.title: 7 · Read the answer
steps.body: One sentence says whether your goal is met, followed by the cost, the biggest risks and anything the study could not work out.

steps.title: 8 · Improve the design
steps.body: The most useful changes the study found. Why shows the evidence; the assistant can make a change for you after you confirm it.

steps.title: 9 · Check what breaks
steps.body: Switches off each piece of equipment in turn, and tests hard conditions, to rank the failures that hurt the site most.

fields.archetype: Planning situation: strong_grid (free import), weak_flexible (capped import, SCR gate, DSR opt-in), off_grid (import islanded).
fields.ens_cap_permyriad: ENS target — the share of energy demand allowed unserved, in ‱ (1 ‱ = 0.01 %). Drives the capacity expansion.
fields.target_lole_h: LOLE target — expected hours per year with unserved load. The Monte-Carlo certifies against it (certified only when the 95 % CI is below it).
fields.import_p_nom_mw: weak_flexible import cap in MW, split equally across the import Links.
fields.import_energy_mwh_per_year: weak_flexible energy import budget in MWh per year, metered at the hub (efficiency × flow) on grid→hub Links, per year of each period.
fields.budget_solves: Ceiling on LP solves across all stages. Stages that would exceed it are skipped with a reason.
fields.mc_draws: Monte-Carlo sample years for certification; more draws narrow the confidence interval.
fields.dsr_buses: weak_flexible only: buses whose demand may be curtailed at a DSR price. Never applied globally.
fields.dtc_attribution: By bus (default): a critical Load makes its whole bus critical. Per Load: each critical Load is reported, non-critical Loads are shed first (5 % VOLL priority, exact on loss-free paths).
fields.levers: Design options priced at the same target: storage_duration, import_cap, import_energy, redundancy.
fields.stages: apply_pack, ens_solve, frontier, mc_certify, fmea_top, redundancy, levers, dtc_stress, dtc_planning, assemble.
fields.frontier: Cost vs availability: re-optimises the plan at several ENS targets around the pack's; the knee is where extra reliability stops paying at your VOLL.
fields.mc_certify: Sequential Monte-Carlo LOLE of the solved plan on the hub side of the boundary; verdict pass / fail / inconclusive.
fields.fmea_top: The five costliest Link failure modes on the plan (Class-B sweep).
fields.redundancy: Compares N, N+1 and spare-unit scenarios for conversion equipment.
fields.dtc_stress: Islands each import on the fixed plan and measures critical vs non-critical unserved energy.
fields.dtc_planning: Re-plans islanded with only critical demand retained; reports the extra capacity and cost.
fields.completeness: ok = evidence produced; skipped = not requested / not applicable; not_established = requested but could not be shown (reason listed).
fields.certification: pass = CI entirely below the target; fail = entirely above; inconclusive = straddles it.
fields.eh_poc: Point of connection: the GRID-side bus of the import boundary. The hub is everything on the other side of the import Links.
fields.eh_critical: Demand on this bus must be served when the import is lost (DtC stress / planning).
fields.eh_sk_mva: Grid short-circuit level at this PoC in MVA — the SCR gate's numerator.
fields.eh_ibr_mva: Inverter-based capacity at this PoC in MVA — the SCR gate's denominator (defaults to installed IBR generators when blank).
fields.eh_role: grid_import = the import the packs cap or island; electrolyser / fuel_cell / conversion = conversion units for redundancy and the multi-energy report.
fields.failure_class: A = generator forced outages (COPT screening); B = Link outages (LP re-solve); C = stress scenarios; D = expert entry.
fields.criticality: Expected cost per year = occurrence (events/yr) × severity (€ per event).
fields.mitigability: Your note on how a mode is mitigated; stored with the project, survives re-solves.
fields.stress_kind: parametric = scale load and renewables; profiles = swap whole series from a pack (names must exist on the network).
fields.frequency_per_year: Empirical events per year of the stress condition, in (0, 365].
fields.renewable_availability_multiplier: Profile-borne generators' availability × this factor, in [0, 1.5]; 0 = no renewable output.
fields.profile_pack: A shipped series pack; its Load/Generator names must exist on your network.
fields.mc_seed: Random seed of the Monte-Carlo sample — fix it to reproduce a certification exactly.
fields.hub_start: Start from a ready-made example site, or use the network you already have.
fields.hub_site: Check what the study needs to know about the site: the grid connection, the load that must stay on, grid strength and how often equipment breaks.
fields.hub_goal: Set how many hours of shortfall per year you can accept, then run the study.
fields.hub_results: Read what the study found: whether the goal is met, what it costs and the biggest risks.
fields.hub_improve: Work through the study's recommendations, check what happens when equipment fails, and add hard conditions to test.
fields.site_type: How the site relates to the grid: a strong grid you can always import from, a weak or limited connection, or no grid connection at all.
fields.grid_connection: The line or transformer that brings power from the public grid to the site, and how much power it can carry.
fields.critical_load: The demand that must keep running even when the grid connection fails, for example servers, operating theatres or cooling.
fields.grid_strength: How strong the public grid is where the site connects. A weak grid limits how much solar, wind and battery equipment the site can safely connect.
fields.outage_data: How often each generator or connection breaks down and how long a repair takes. The study needs this to estimate shortfall.
fields.shortfall_hours: Expected hours per year when some demand cannot be served. Lower is more reliable; the study checks the site against your goal.
fields.energy_strictness: How much of the yearly energy demand may go unserved at most, as a very small share. Stricter means more backup equipment and higher cost.
fields.verdict: The study's answer: certified (the goal is met), not certified (it is missed), not decided (more random trials are needed) or no goal set (nothing to check against).
fields.cost_at_target: The yearly cost of the planned design, including new equipment and running costs. It leaves out the cost of any shortfall; the verdict above says how reliable the design is.
fields.top_risks: The failures that cost the most per year, combining how often they happen with how much damage each one does.
fields.not_established: Parts of the study that could not be worked out, with the reason, so you know what the result does not cover.
fields.stress_scenario: A hard condition to test the site against, such as a heatwave or a dark, windless week, with how often it happens.
fields.fmea_check: A check that switches off each piece of equipment in turn and in stress conditions, to find the failures that hurt the site most.
fields.template_provenance: Where the example site's numbers come from. Example sites use made-up but realistic data, so replace them with your own before deciding.
fields.voll_plain: What each unit of energy that cannot be delivered is worth to you, in euros. The study needs a price above zero to weigh shortfall against the cost of backup.
fields.fmea_class_a: A generator breaks down at random. The row estimates how often that happens and what the missing energy would cost, without re-running the whole plan.
fields.fmea_class_b: A connection, such as the grid supply or a converter, is switched off and the plan is re-run to measure the energy the site cannot get.
fields.fmea_class_c: A hard condition you described, such as a heatwave or a dark, windless week, is applied and the plan is re-run to measure the shortfall.
fields.fmea_class_d: A failure you added yourself, with your own estimate of how often it happens and what one event costs. It is kept with the project.
fields.fmea_engine: How this row was worked out: a quick estimate for a generator, a full re-run of the plan for connections and stress scenarios, or your own figures.
fields.fmea_severity: What one event costs: the energy that cannot be delivered, priced at what undelivered energy is worth to you.
fields.fmea_occurrence: How often the failure happens, in events per year. For equipment it comes from how often it breaks down and how long a repair takes.
fields.fmea_criticality: The yearly risk: how often the failure happens times what one event costs. The table is ranked by it, largest first.
fields.mwh: A megawatt-hour: the energy of one megawatt of power delivered for one hour, the same as 1 000 kilowatt-hours.
